title: 1 Samuel 30:1–6
context: Returning to Ziklag after being sent away from the Philistine army, David and his men find that Amalekites have raided and burned the town and carried off the women and children, including David’s two wives. The men weep until they can weep no more and talk of stoning David, but David strengthens himself in the LORD his God. Both traditions read this as shared ground on finding strength in God amid loss and blame.

verses.text: When David and his men had come to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid on the South and on Ziklag, and had struck Ziklag and burned it with fire,
verses.arminianNotes:
David and his men reach Ziklag on the third day and find it raided and burned by the Amalekites. Arminian readers note the setting: David has just been sent away from the Philistine army (1 Sam 29), and he returns to disaster at home.

Ziklag had been given to David by Achish (1 Sam 27:6), so the loss strikes at his place of refuge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s providence in the timing. David’s dismissal from the Philistine ranks spares him from fighting Israel and brings him back in time to pursue the raiders.

The Amalekites, whom Saul had failed to destroy (1 Sam 15), now strike David’s household.

verses.text: and had taken captive the women and all who were in it, both small and great. They didn’t kill any, but carried them off and went their way.
verses.arminianNotes:
The raiders take the women and everyone in the town captive, both small and great, but kill no one. Arminian readers note that this detail leaves room for rescue and hope.

The raiders likely intended to sell or keep the captives, though the text simply says they carried them off.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s restraining providence in the fact that no one was killed.

The detail prepares for the full recovery promised in verse 8 and reported in verses 18–19. God preserves what he intends to restore.

verses.text: When David and his men came to the city, behold, it was burned with fire; and their wives, their sons, and their daughters were taken captive.
verses.arminianNotes:
David and his men find the city burned and their wives, sons, and daughters taken. Arminian readers note the personal weight of the loss: every family is affected.

The narrator lets the scene speak through what the men see.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a real trial in which David’s faith will be tested alongside his leadership.

The burned town and empty homes show how quickly earthly security can disappear. The text records the loss without softening it.

verses.text: Then David and the people who were with him lifted up their voice and wept until they had no more power to weep.
verses.arminianNotes:
David and the people weep until they have no more power to weep. Arminian readers note that Scripture gives room for honest, exhausting grief.

Faith does not require hiding sorrow; David weeps with his men.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see grief as a fitting response to real loss, voiced openly as in many psalms.

The tears of the leader and his men show that strong people may be brought to the end of their strength before God acts.

verses.text: David’s two wives were taken captive, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
verses.arminianNotes:
David’s two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail, are among the captives. Arminian readers note that David shares the same loss as his men.

He is not spared the pain of those he leads.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the leader standing in solidarity with his people’s suffering.

Abigail’s earlier story (1 Sam 25) and Ahinoam’s mention keep the narrative personal. The loss touches David’s own household directly.

verses.text: David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because the souls of all the people were grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters; but David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people speak of stoning David in their grief, “but David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.” Arminian readers note that David turns to God in a moment when he could have turned to blame or despair.

Jonathan had earlier strengthened David’s hand in God (1 Sam 23:16); now David must find that strength himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the turning point of the chapter in this phrase. Strength is found in the LORD, not in circumstances or popularity.

Both traditions treat the verse as shared ground and a pastoral model for those who face loss and blame (cf. Ps 42:5; Hab 3:17–18).
